h1: Top 30 Car Companies by Revenue and Profit (2025 Archive)

contentBlocks.text: The car industry's money reports for 2025 show one harsh truth: choosing the right engine technology was way more important than just throwing money around. For a long time, everyone in the industry thought the main goal was to sell as many EVs as possible, no matter the cost. But the numbers from 2025 completely changed that idea.

Take Volkswagen, for example. They still made the most money globally, bringing in a huge $351 billion. But they spent so much money pushing hard into EVs that their profit margin ended up pretty low, only 3.5%. Now, look at Toyota. They focused on their hybrid cars (HEVs and PHEVs) instead. This really hit what people wanted when excitement for pure EVs started to calm down. What happened? They made an amazing $31.2 billion in profit. That's two and a half times more cash than Volkswagen, and with a great profit margin of 9.9%.

Big, older car makers in Detroit and Europe got a rude awakening. Even though EV sales worldwide still went up by about 20% and made up 25% of all cars sold, profits quickly went down. Companies that put too much into just pure-EV platforms found they had spread themselves too thin. Stellantis (3.5% profit), GM (3.2%), and Ford (3.2%) all made some profit, but they had a really tough time in North America. Expensive EVs just sat on dealership lots, which forced them to cut prices. This really hurt their profits.
The rankings below break down the top 30 global car companies by 2024 revenue, with net profit margins added for direct comparison.

2025 was also a big year because BYD officially made more money than Tesla overall, taking in $108 billion compared to Tesla's $97.6 billion. This isn't just about who's bigger; it shows how two very different ways of making cars from start to finish are competing. For example, BYD had revenue of $108 billion and profit of $5.6 billion, giving them a 5.2% profit margin. Tesla, on the other hand, had $97.7 billion in revenue and made $7.1 billion in profit, with a higher margin of 7.3%.

Tesla cut prices all over the world to keep its factories busy. This pushed its profit margin down to 7.3%, which is much lower than before, even if it's still pretty good. BYD, however, made almost all its parts itself. This helped them handle the price wars better and still get a 5.2% profit margin, showing they can compete with Tesla globally.
Who Did Well and Who Didn't During This Change.

Nissan was the older brand that got hurt the most in 2025. They lost a huge $4.4 billion, and their profit margin dropped to -5.3%. Nissan struggled because they just didn't have the right products or technology. In key markets like the US and China, they couldn't compete with Toyota's hybrids and didn't have any good plug-in hybrid options.

On the other hand, Suzuki handled things really smartly. They didn't waste billions on self-driving tech or pure EVs. Instead, they focused on markets where they were strong, like India. By making their small gas engines and mild hybrids cheaper, Suzuki got an amazing 7.1% profit margin without spending a lot of money. When the economy was bad, offering cars that were dependable and affordable turned out to be a huge advantage.

The financial reports from 2025 show that the car industry doesn't care about big ideas anymore. What matters is making the right products well and being smart with money. The time of putting all your money on one type of engine or just cutting prices to gain customers is gone. The future will be for car makers who are flexible, have different engine options, and can quickly change what they make to match what people want.
